title: Output with external damage
prompt: Inverse demand is 100 − Q, private marginal cost is 20, and marginal external damage is 20. What output maximizes total surplus?
correct: 60 units.
wrong: 80 units.
40 units.
30 units.
explanation: Social marginal cost is 20 + 20 = 40. Equating demand to social marginal cost gives 100 − Q = 40, hence Q = 60. Private choice would produce 80.
hint: Add external damage to private marginal cost before comparing with demand.

title: Efficient abatement
prompt: Marginal benefit of abatement is 80 − 2A and marginal abatement cost is 2A, with 0 ≤ A ≤ 40. What is efficient abatement?
correct: 20 units.
wrong: 40 units.
0 units.
10 units.
explanation: At an interior optimum, 80 − 2A = 2A, giving A = 20. Zero or complete abatement ignores the marginal tradeoff.
hint: Equate the benefit and cost of the next unit abated.

title: Damage at the margin
prompt: Total environmental damage from emissions E is D(E) = 3E². At E = 5, what is marginal damage?
correct: 30 currency units per emission unit.
wrong: 75 currency units per emission unit.
15 currency units per emission unit.
6 currency units per emission unit.
explanation: The derivative is D′(E) = 6E, so marginal damage is 30. Total damage is 75 and average damage is 15.
hint: Differentiate the damage function before substituting emissions.

title: Public environmental benefits
prompt: Two residents have marginal willingness to pay 12 − G and 8 − G for the same public cleanup G, for 0 ≤ G ≤ 8. Marginal cost is 10. What is efficient G?
correct: 5 units.
wrong: 1 unit.
10 units.
3 units.
explanation: Both enjoy the same quantity, so marginal benefits sum to 20 − 2G. Equating this to 10 gives G = 5.
hint: Sum willingness to pay vertically at the same cleanup quantity.

title: Bargaining over a filter
prompt: A factory can install a filter costing 70 that prevents 100 of harm to its sole neighbor. The factory initially has a right to pollute; bargaining is costless and transfers are feasible. Which agreement can make both better off?
correct: The neighbor pays 85 for the factory to install the filter.
wrong: The factory pays the neighbor 85 and installs the filter.
The neighbor pays 50 for the filter, which the factory voluntarily accepts.
No agreement is possible because the factory holds the pollution right.
explanation: A payment between 70 and 100 covers the filter cost and is less than the avoided harm. At 85, each party gains 15 relative to no filter and no transfer.
hint: Find the interval between the factory’s cost and the neighbor’s benefit.

title: Property rights and distribution
prompt: Costless bargaining over a nuisance achieves the same efficient noise level under either initial legal entitlement. Why can residents still care which entitlement the law assigns?
correct: Entitlements change the bargaining baseline and transfers.
wrong: Efficiency implies every participant receives the same income under both rules.
A legal entitlement mechanically changes the physical noise technology.
Transfers disappear whenever bargaining is efficient.
explanation: An invariant efficient allocation does not imply an invariant wealth distribution. The entitlement determines who can demand compensation.
hint: Compare the fallback positions when no bargain is reached.

title: Cost of excessive output
prompt: Demand is 100 − Q, private marginal cost is 20, and marginal external damage is 20. Unregulated output is 80 and efficient output is 60. What is the surplus loss from excess output?
correct: 200 currency units.
wrong: 400 currency units.
1,600 currency units.
20 currency units.
explanation: The wedge between social marginal cost and marginal benefit rises linearly from 0 to 20 over 20 excess units. Its triangle area is 20 × 20 / 2 = 200.
hint: Integrate the social marginal cost minus benefit only over excess output.

title: A pecuniary effect
prompt: A new shop raises demand for nearby land, increasing rents, but creates no pollution or other unpriced spillovers. With competitive complete markets, why is the rent increase alone insufficient evidence of market failure?
correct: It is a price-mediated effect, not necessarily an unpriced social cost.
wrong: All effects on third parties are external costs requiring taxes.
Higher rents are never paid by anyone.
Land scarcity cannot affect economic welfare.
explanation: A change operating through competitive prices redistributes surplus and conveys scarcity. It differs from an unpriced technological externality.
hint: Ask whether the effect occurs through a market price.

title: Spatial emissions
prompt: Two plants each emit one ton, but exposure modeling gives marginal damages of 90 near plant A and 10 near plant B. What does this imply for a damage-based tax?
correct: Different per-ton rates can be efficient because damages depend on location.
wrong: Every pollutant must have the same per-ton tax everywhere.
Plant A should face the lower tax because its existing damage is larger.
Only total national emissions matter for any pollutant.
explanation: Equal physical emissions need not cause equal exposure or harm. A differentiated tax can reflect source-specific marginal damage.
hint: Distinguish a ton emitted from the harm it causes.

title: Optimal residual pollution
prompt: The last unit of pollution could be removed for 500 but would avoid only 40 in damage; all other effects are included. Should that unit be removed on surplus grounds?
correct: No; removing it reduces surplus by 460.
wrong: Yes; zero pollution always maximizes surplus.
Yes; any positive damage makes removal efficient.
No; abatement costs are transfers and therefore irrelevant.
explanation: The incremental benefit is 40 and real resource cost is 500. A positive residual emission can be efficient when further abatement costs more than it benefits.
hint: Compare incremental avoided harm with incremental real cost.

title: Allocating a cleanup target
prompt: Two firms must jointly abate 12 units. Their marginal abatement costs are 2a and 4b, respectively, with a + b = 12 and no binding capacity limits. What minimizes total cost?
correct: a = 8 and b = 4.
wrong: a = 6 and b = 6.
a = 4 and b = 8.
a = 12 and b = 0.
explanation: Cost minimization requires 2a = 4b. Combining a = 2b with the target gives b = 4 and a = 8.
hint: Use both the common marginal cost condition and the total target.

title: Response to an emissions tax
prompt: A firm initially emits 10 units and can abate A at total cost A². A tax of 12 applies to each remaining emission unit. What abatement minimizes its cost?
correct: 6 units.
wrong: 10 units.
12 units.
3 units.
explanation: The firm equates marginal abatement cost 2A to the tax 12, yielding A = 6 within the feasible range.
hint: Compare the tax saved by one more abatement unit with marginal abatement cost.

title: Grandfathered permits
prompt: A firm receives freely transferable permits for free in a competitive market. A permit sells for 25. What is the opportunity cost of using one permit?
correct: 25, because the firm forgoes selling it.
wrong: Zero, because its purchase price was zero.
50, because both buying and selling prices must be counted.
Its historical emissions, regardless of the market price.
explanation: Using a tradable permit sacrifices sale revenue. Free allocation affects wealth but does not eliminate the marginal emissions incentive.
hint: What could the firm receive by selling rather than using the permit?

title: Tax and cap under certainty
prompt: The regulator knows all costs and damages, firms are competitive, enforcement is perfect, and transaction costs are zero. A tax induces exactly the emissions allowed by a cap with competitively traded permits. What follows?
correct: Both can implement the same emissions allocation and abatement cost.
wrong: A cap necessarily causes greater abatement cost because permits are scarce.
A tax necessarily produces zero emissions.
Free allocation necessarily eliminates the cap’s incentive to abate.
explanation: With equivalent emissions and common marginal incentives, the instruments can produce the same cost-minimizing allocation. Their revenue distribution can differ.
hint: Separate marginal incentives from who receives revenue.

title: Uncertain abatement costs
prompt: In the standard local linear-quadratic price-versus-quantity model, uncertainty shifts marginal abatement cost, marginal benefits are relatively flat, and marginal costs are steep. Which instrument is favored in expected surplus terms?
correct: A fixed abatement incentive price.
wrong: A fixed abatement quantity in every such case.
Either instrument must achieve the ex post optimum.
A complete ban regardless of cost.
explanation: When benefits vary little with quantity while costs vary steeply, allowing quantity to respond to cost shocks avoids costly quantity rigidity. This conclusion uses the stated standard uncertainty model.
hint: Compare the welfare loss from quantity error with the loss from forcing costly abatement.

title: A steep damage threshold
prompt: A pollutant causes sharply increasing marginal damage near a known emissions threshold, while marginal abatement cost is uncertain and comparatively flat. In the local price-versus-quantity comparison, what favors a cap?
correct: It limits quantity errors where marginal damage changes rapidly.
wrong: It guarantees the lowest realized marginal cost.
It makes damages independent of emissions.
It eliminates uncertainty about the permit price.
explanation: A steep marginal damage schedule makes emissions deviations costly. A quantity limit controls that margin, although its compliance price can vary.
hint: Which outcome does a cap fix directly?

title: Permit price ceiling
prompt: A regulator sells unlimited additional allowances at 50 while initially issuing a fixed number of allowances. What tradeoff does this create?
correct: The price is limited, but emissions may exceed the initial allowance quantity.
wrong: Both price and emissions are fixed at their original limits in all states.
The price ceiling necessarily reduces emissions below the initial cap.
Extra allowance sales cannot affect aggregate compliance emissions.
explanation: Additional supply at 50 prevents higher compliance prices under the stated rules, but permits emissions beyond the original supply.
hint: Count the extra allowances sold when demand is high.

title: Expected enforcement cost
prompt: Each unreported emission unit has an independent 0.2 detection probability and incurs a fine of 100 if detected. A risk-neutral firm can prevent that unit at cost 15. With no other consequences, what does it prefer?
correct: Prevent the unit, since 15 is below expected fine 20.
wrong: Emit the unit, since detection is less than certain.
Emit the unit, since 15 exceeds detection probability 0.2.
Prevent the unit only if cost falls below 5.
explanation: Expected fine is 0.2 × 100 = 20. Abatement costing 15 is cheaper for a risk-neutral decision-maker.
hint: Multiply the detection probability by the conditional fine.

title: Emissions-rate standard
prompt: A plant meets a standard of at most 0.5 tons per unit of output. It doubles output from 100 to 200 while remaining exactly at the standard. What happens to emissions?
correct: They rise from 50 to 100 tons.
wrong: They remain fixed at 50 tons.
They fall from 100 to 50 tons.
They are zero because the standard is satisfied.
explanation: An intensity limit constrains emissions per output, not total output. At the binding rate, emissions equal 0.5 times output.
hint: Multiply the emissions rate by each output quantity.

title: Tradable emissions with local harm
prompt: Two sources have different local marginal damages, but a permit system treats their emissions as perfect substitutes one for one. What is the central efficiency concern?
correct: A trade can lower abatement cost while increasing total environmental damage.
wrong: Every trade necessarily increases both sources’ emissions.
Trading cannot equalize marginal abatement costs.
Local damages must be equal because permits have one price.
explanation: Uniform trading equalizes abatement costs for the aggregate target. When source damages differ, that target alone does not ensure the spatial allocation maximizes surplus.
hint: Track both where emissions move and what abatement costs are saved.

title: Recreation surplus
prompt: Annual park visits follow V = 12 − 2p for generalized trip price p between 0 and 6. At p = 2, what is annual consumer surplus under this linear demand?
correct: 16 currency units.
wrong: 8 currency units.
32 currency units.
24 currency units.
explanation: There are 8 visits, and the choke price is 6. The surplus triangle is (6 − 2) × 8 / 2 = 16.
hint: Find the choke price and the triangle above the paid price.

title: Time in travel cost
prompt: Two visitors pay the same fuel cost but one spends three more hours traveling. Why might fuel expenditure alone mismeasure the visit price?
correct: Travel time can have an opportunity cost.
wrong: Travel time must be valued at zero because no ticket is sold for it.
All visitors necessarily value an hour equally.
Longer trips prove higher environmental quality.
explanation: Generalized travel cost includes relevant time costs as well as money costs. The appropriate time value requires assumptions or evidence, not automatic equality across visitors.
hint: Consider what the visitor gives up while traveling.

title: Housing price gradient
prompt: An analyst observes that cleaner neighborhoods have higher house prices. Why is this correlation alone insufficient to identify willingness to pay for clean air?
correct: School quality and other amenities may covary with air quality.
wrong: Housing prices cannot reflect environmental amenities.
Willingness to pay is always zero for goods without separate markets.
A positive correlation is already a randomized air-quality experiment.
explanation: Hedonic identification must account for correlated attributes and sorting. A raw price difference can combine air quality with other valued neighborhood features.
hint: List other features that differ across neighborhoods.

title: Nonuse benefits
prompt: A resident would pay to preserve a distant species despite never expecting to see it. Which valuation approach can in principle elicit this nonuse value?
correct: A carefully designed stated-preference survey.
wrong: A travel-cost study restricted to actual visitors, by itself.
A count of visits multiplied by zero travel cost.
The species’ commercial harvest revenue alone.
explanation: Stated-preference methods can ask about willingness to pay for preservation independent of use. Behavioral market measures limited to visits or harvest miss this stated nonuse motive.
hint: Look for a method that can ask nonusers about preservation.

title: Hypothetical payment
prompt: A survey asks respondents whether they support cleanup but mentions no required payment or budget consequence. Why is the support share not directly a monetary benefit estimate?
correct: Support does not reveal the amount respondents would give up.
wrong: Any majority vote reveals infinite willingness to pay.
Nonmarket benefits have no monetary equivalent.
Support shares always equal average willingness to pay in dollars.
explanation: Monetary valuation requires a tradeoff against resources, typically via a credible payment mechanism. Costless approval alone does not measure that tradeoff.
hint: Identify the budget tradeoff in the survey question.

title: Adding household benefits
prompt: A hypothetical representative study estimates mean annual household willingness to pay of 18 for a cleanup. There are 2,000 covered households, each counted once. What annual aggregate benefit follows?
correct: 36,000 currency units.
wrong: 18 currency units.
111.11 currency units.
72,000 currency units.
explanation: Multiply household willingness to pay by the number of relevant households: 18 × 2,000 = 36,000. The estimate is annual and must not be treated as a perpetual lump sum.
hint: Keep the household unit and annual time period consistent.

title: Avoiding double counting
prompt: A clean-air benefit estimate already includes residents’ willingness to pay for reduced illness, including their expected medical spending savings. What happens if those same savings are added again?
correct: The same benefit is counted twice.
wrong: The estimate becomes more conservative.
All medical costs are transfers and can never be benefits.
The willingness-to-pay estimate must be discarded because health is involved.
explanation: The stipulated willingness-to-pay measure already incorporates those savings. Adding them separately duplicates the same welfare component.
hint: Check what the first benefit measure already includes.

title: Small risk reductions
prompt: Each of 1,000 people would pay 30 for an annual mortality-risk reduction of 1 in 100,000. What value of a statistical life is implied by this marginal tradeoff?
correct: 3,000,000 currency units.
wrong: 30,000 currency units.
3,000 currency units.
100,000 currency units.
explanation: Individual willingness to pay divided by the risk reduction is 30 / 0.00001 = 3,000,000. Equivalently aggregate payment 30,000 buys 0.01 expected lives saved.
hint: Divide willingness to pay by the probability reduction, not the population.

title: Transferring a valuation
prompt: A study estimates recreation benefits at a lake with many close substitutes. A proposed site has no close substitutes and serves a different-income population. What is the strongest assessment?
correct: Directly transferring the estimate requires justification for these differences.
wrong: The original estimate must be exactly correct at every lake.
Having fewer substitutes guarantees that the original estimate is too high.
Benefit transfer is impossible even after justified adjustments.
explanation: Substitution possibilities and income affect demand and willingness to pay. These differences warrant adjustment or new evidence; they do not alone provide an exact correction.
hint: Compare the determinants of demand across source and target sites.

title: Preservation before learning
prompt: A habitat can be preserved for one year while information about its value arrives, but development now would destroy it irreversibly. What benefit can waiting provide?
correct: The option to condition the later decision on new information.
wrong: A guarantee that preservation will ultimately be optimal.
A reason to ignore the cost of delaying development.
A benefit only if development can be fully reversed.
explanation: Waiting can preserve a choice that learning will improve. Its value must be weighed against delay costs and does not guarantee permanent preservation.
hint: Compare the decisions still available after information arrives.

title: Carbon stock dynamics
prompt: A simplified atmospheric stock follows S next = 0.9S now + E. If S now is 100 and emissions E are 20, what is next period’s stock?
correct: 110 units.
wrong: 120 units.
90 units.
20 units.
explanation: Ninety units remain from the existing stock and 20 are added, so the next stock is 110. Emissions are a flow rather than the whole stock.
hint: Add new emissions after applying the retention fraction to the stock.

title: Stabilizing the stock
prompt: A simplified carbon stock follows S next = 0.95S now + E. At a constant stock of 200, what constant emissions flow maintains that stock?
correct: 10 units per period.
wrong: 200 units per period.
190 units per period.
Zero is the only possible answer in this model.
explanation: At a steady state, E = (1 − 0.95) × 200 = 10. This result belongs to the stipulated one-box decay model, not a claim about actual carbon-cycle stabilization.
hint: Set next period’s stock equal to today’s stock.

title: Global marginal climate damage
prompt: One extra ton causes present-value damages of 12 domestically and 28 abroad, with no other effects. What marginal damage enters a global surplus calculation?
correct: 40 currency units per ton.
wrong: 12 currency units per ton.
28 currency units per ton.
16 currency units per ton.
explanation: A global perspective sums domestic and foreign damage: 12 + 28 = 40. A domestic-only objective would use a different scope.
hint: Match the geographic scope of damages to the objective.

title: Discounting future climate benefits
prompt: A project yields a single certain benefit of 121 in two years. At an annual discount rate of 10%, what is its present value?
correct: 100 currency units.
wrong: 110 currency units.
121 currency units.
146.41 currency units.
explanation: Present value is 121 / 1.1² = 100. Compounding moves values forward; discounting moves them back.
hint: Divide by the compounded two-year discount factor.

title: Discount-rate sensitivity
prompt: Two policies have identical present costs. One prevents damage next year; the other prevents the same monetary damage in 100 years. What does increasing a positive discount rate do to the relative present value of the latter benefit?
correct: It reduces it relative to the near-term benefit.
wrong: It raises it relative to the near-term benefit.
It leaves the ratio unchanged because the undiscounted amounts match.
It makes the distant benefit negative.
explanation: The ratio of discounted distant to near benefits is (1 + r)^−99, decreasing in r. Discounting reduces positive benefits without changing their sign.
hint: Compare the exponents in the two discount factors.

title: International free riding
prompt: Each of two countries can abate at cost 6. Each country’s abatement benefits itself by 4 and the other country by 4. Actions and effects add. What happens with selfish noncooperative choice versus joint surplus maximization?
correct: Neither abates noncooperatively; joint surplus favors both abating.
wrong: Both abate noncooperatively because global benefit is 8.
Neither abates under either objective because private cost exceeds private benefit.
Exactly one must abate under joint surplus maximization.
explanation: Each unilateral action gives its actor 4 − 6 = −2, but global net benefit is 4 + 4 − 6 = 2. The additive joint optimum adopts both.
hint: Separate own benefits from benefits received abroad.

title: Emissions leakage
prompt: A domestic policy cuts home emissions by 100 tons but induces 30 extra tons abroad. Relative to no policy, what is the global reduction and leakage rate?
correct: 70 tons and 30%.
wrong: 130 tons and 30%.
70 tons and 70%.
100 tons and 0%.
explanation: Net reduction is 100 − 30 = 70; leakage is the induced foreign increase divided by the domestic reduction, 30/100 = 30%.
hint: Subtract displaced emissions and use the domestic reduction as the denominator.

title: Offsets and additionality
prompt: A forest would have remained intact without an offset payment. A program nevertheless awards credits for its unchanged carbon stock, with no other behavioral changes. What is the additionality problem?
correct: The credited action causes no extra carbon preservation relative to the baseline.
wrong: Existing forest carbon cannot physically exist.
Any payment automatically makes preservation additional.
Additionality concerns only the timing of credit sales.
explanation: Additionality compares outcomes with and without the intervention. Paying for the same baseline outcome does not create the credited incremental reduction.
hint: Compare preservation under the program with preservation without it.

title: Adaptation and mitigation
prompt: A seawall reduces local flood damage but leaves emissions unchanged. A separate intervention lowers emissions but has no direct local protection effect. Which classification is correct?
correct: The seawall is adaptation; the emissions reduction is mitigation.
wrong: Both are mitigation because both can reduce climate losses.
The seawall is mitigation; the emissions reduction is adaptation.
Neither can have economic benefits unless it does both.
explanation: Adaptation reduces vulnerability to climate effects; mitigation reduces climate forcing through emissions or related channels. The measures can complement each other.
hint: Ask whether the intervention changes exposure to harm or the climate driver.

title: Efficiency and the rebound effect
prompt: An appliance upgrade would save 40 energy units at unchanged use. Lower operating cost induces more use consuming 10 of those units. What is the realized saving and direct rebound fraction?
correct: 30 units and 25%.
wrong: 50 units and 25%.
30 units and 75%.
10 units and 100%.
explanation: Realized saving is 40 − 10 = 30. Rebound is lost engineering saving divided by engineering saving: 10/40 = 25%.
hint: Measure the behavioral giveback against the engineering saving.

title: Scarcity rent growth
prompt: An exhaustible-resource owner faces constant marginal extraction cost of 10. Current competitive price is 30. Under the deterministic interior Hotelling rule with a 5% interest rate and no stock-dependent costs, what is next period’s price?
correct: 31 currency units.
wrong: 31.50 currency units.
21 currency units.
30 currency units.
explanation: Current scarcity rent is 30 − 10 = 20. Rent grows to 21, so price becomes 10 + 21 = 31. The rule applies to net price, not gross price.
hint: Grow price minus marginal extraction cost at the interest rate.

title: Two-period resource allocation
prompt: An owner allocates a stock of 10 between two periods. Marginal net benefits are 20 − q1 and 20 − q2; the discount rate is zero. What efficient allocation exhausts the stock?
correct: q1 = 5 and q2 = 5.
wrong: q1 = 2 and q2 = 8.
explanation: Equal undiscounted marginal net benefits require q1 = q2. The stock constraint then gives 5 units in each period.
hint: Use equal marginal net benefits together with the stock constraint.

title: Discounted extraction incentive
prompt: In a two-period resource model at the current allocation, marginal net benefit is 10 today and 12 next period. The discount rate is 10%, and a small unit can be shifted without violating constraints. Which shift raises present surplus?
correct: Move a small unit of extraction from today to next period.
wrong: Move a small unit from next period to today.
Neither shift matters because both periods use the same resource.
Extract an extra unit in both periods despite a fixed binding stock.
explanation: Next period’s marginal benefit is worth 12/1.1 ≈ 10.91 today, exceeding 10. Delaying a small unit raises present surplus until marginal conditions adjust.
hint: Discount next period’s marginal benefit before comparing it with today’s.

title: Backstop substitution
prompt: A perfect substitute for an exhaustible resource is available in unlimited quantity at constant delivered cost 50. There are no switching costs or quality differences. What constrains the resource’s competitive delivered price?
correct: Consumers will switch if it exceeds 50.
wrong: Scarcity permits the resource price to exceed 50 indefinitely without substitution.
The resource price must equal zero immediately.
The substitute eliminates all past extraction costs.
explanation: An unlimited perfect substitute at 50 gives buyers an alternative. A higher resource price cannot persist with positive demand under these assumptions.
hint: Compare identical services at their delivered prices.

title: Logistic resource growth
prompt: A fish stock X grows by G(X) = 0.2X(1 − X/100). At which stock is natural growth largest?
explanation: The symmetric concave quadratic peaks at half carrying capacity, X = 50, where growth is 5. Maximum standing stock is not maximum growth.
hint: Locate the vertex of the biological growth function.

title: Harvest above current growth
prompt: A fishery starts with stock 80. During the period natural growth adds 12 and harvest removes 18, with no other flows. What is the ending stock?
correct: 74 units.
wrong: 86 units.
98 units.
62 units.
explanation: Stock accounting gives 80 + 12 − 18 = 74. Harvest exceeds growth by 6, so stock declines by 6.
hint: Add natural growth and subtract harvest from the starting stock.

title: Open-access entry
prompt: Fishers can enter freely, all opportunity costs are included, and positive economic profits attract entry. What condition characterizes an interior static open-access equilibrium?
correct: Total revenue equals total opportunity cost.
wrong: Marginal revenue necessarily equals marginal social cost at the efficient stock.
Economic profit is maximized across all fishers.
Natural growth must be zero.
explanation: Entry dissipates economic rent until no entrant can earn positive economic profit. Zero-profit open access generally differs from a rent-maximizing managed fishery.
hint: Ask what removes the incentive for another fisher to enter.

title: Economic versus biological yield
prompt: A fishery manager can sustain harvest 20 at cost 190 or harvest 16 at cost 100. Fish sells for 10 per unit, with no other benefits or costs. Which option yields more annual economic rent?
correct: Harvest 16, yielding rent 60 instead of 10.
wrong: Harvest 20, yielding rent 200 instead of 160.
Both yield the same rent because both are sustainable.
Harvest 20, because maximum harvest always maximizes rent.
explanation: Rent subtracts real costs from revenue. The options yield 200 − 190 = 10 and 160 − 100 = 60. Biological output does not by itself rank economic returns.
hint: Subtract cost from harvest revenue for each option.

title: Shared aquifer pumping
prompt: One farmer’s pumping lowers the water table and raises neighbors’ future pumping costs, which the farmer does not bear. What incentive distortion follows?
correct: Private pumping ignores part of its marginal social cost.
wrong: The lower water table automatically compensates neighbors.
Future costs cannot matter for current efficiency.
Private pumping necessarily falls below the efficient level because extraction has a cost.
explanation: The farmer neglects the imposed future cost. This stock externality can create excessive pumping relative to the social optimum.
hint: Track whose future extraction costs increase after one more unit is pumped.

title: A one-year forest decision
prompt: A stand can be sold now for 1,000 or with certainty for 1,080 next year. There are no other forest services, costs, or later choices; the discount rate is 10%. Which action has higher present value?
correct: Sell now; waiting is worth about 981.82 today.
wrong: Wait; 1,080 exceeds 1,000 without discounting.
Either choice has the same value because both are positive.
Wait; discounting makes future revenue larger today.
explanation: The delayed sale is worth 1,080/1.1 ≈ 981.82, below 1,000. This one-time choice excludes replanting and non-timber services.
hint: Discount next year’s sale value and compare it with today’s proceeds.

title: Net present environmental benefits
prompt: A cleanup costs 100 now and yields certain benefits of 60 after one year and 60 after two years. At 10%, what is its net present value, rounded to two decimals?
correct: 4.13 currency units.
wrong: 20.00 currency units.
9.09 currency units.
−0.83 currency units.
explanation: NPV = −100 + 60/1.1 + 60/1.1² ≈ 4.13. Both benefits must be discounted from their own dates.
hint: Discount each benefit separately before subtracting the current cost.

title: Potential compensation
prompt: A policy gives one group a monetary benefit of 150 and imposes a cost of 100 on another. No compensation is paid. What does a positive unweighted net benefit establish?
correct: Winners could compensate losers and retain a gain, but actual Pareto improvement is not established.
wrong: Everyone is better off because 150 exceeds 100.
Losers have necessarily received 100.
The policy fails every possible efficiency criterion.
explanation: The surplus is 50, so hypothetical compensation is feasible in the monetary comparison. Without compensation, the losing group remains worse off.
hint: Ask whether the transfer is feasible or actually made.

title: Distributional weights
prompt: A policy gives a lower-income group a benefit of 40 and imposes a higher-income group cost of 60. The evaluator explicitly weights their monetary changes by 2 and 1 respectively. What is weighted net benefit?
correct: 20 currency units in the weighted objective.
wrong: −20 currency units in the weighted objective.
100 currency units in the weighted objective.
−80 currency units in the weighted objective.
explanation: The stated objective gives 2 × 40 − 1 × 60 = 20. Unweighted net benefit is −20, illustrating the role of the chosen welfare weights.
hint: Multiply each group’s signed benefit by its assigned weight.

title: Revenue recycling
prompt: A household pays 300 in higher annual fuel bills because of a carbon policy and receives a 350 lump-sum rebate. Ignoring all other changes, what is its direct net monetary effect?
correct: A gain of 50.
wrong: A loss of 300.
A gain of 350.
A loss of 650.
explanation: The rebate minus the bill increase is 350 − 300 = 50. This narrow calculation does not include health effects, behavioral surplus, or other income changes.
hint: Include both the household’s payment and its rebate.

title: Physical exposure and burden
prompt: A policy reduces average city pollution but raises exposure in one already highly exposed neighborhood. Which claim is supported by those facts alone?
correct: Average improvement can coexist with a worsening local exposure distribution.
wrong: Every resident’s health risk must fall.
The policy must have negative total net benefit.
The neighborhood must receive sufficient compensation.
explanation: An aggregate average does not determine every group’s outcome. The facts identify a distributional concern without supplying enough information for a full net-benefit ranking.
hint: Distinguish the citywide mean from neighborhood-specific changes.

title: Taxes in social accounting
prompt: Firms pay 200 in emissions taxes to the domestic government. A domestic cost-benefit analysis counts both firms and government with equal monetary weights. Ignoring collection costs and behavioral effects, how should this payment enter net social cost?
correct: As an offsetting transfer, not a net resource cost of 200.
wrong: As 200 of firm cost with government receipts omitted.
As 400 of cost because both sides handle the payment.
As 200 of benefit with firm payments omitted.
explanation: The payment is a loss to firms and an equal receipt to government within the same boundary. Real abatement, administration, and distortion effects require separate accounting.
hint: Include both sides of the same domestic payment.

title: Difference-in-differences cleanup evaluation
prompt: Pollution falls from 80 to 50 in a regulated city and from 70 to 60 in an untreated comparison city. Under parallel untreated trends, no anticipation and no spillovers, what is the estimated regulation effect?
correct: A reduction of 20 pollution units.
wrong: A reduction of 30 pollution units.
A reduction of 10 pollution units.
An increase of 20 pollution units.
explanation: The treated change is −30 and the comparison change is −10. The difference is −30 − (−10) = −20. The causal reading requires the stated assumptions.
skill: estimate policy effect with a comparison group
hint: Subtract the comparison city’s change from the regulated city’s change.

title: Anticipation before regulation
prompt: Firms begin installing filters after a policy announcement, one year before legal enforcement. An analyst labels that year untreated. What identification concern arises?
correct: The supposed pre-treatment period already contains behavioral treatment responses.
wrong: Only the enforcement date can ever affect behavior.
Anticipation guarantees the estimate has the correct sign and magnitude.
A longer panel automatically removes anticipation bias.
explanation: Behavior can respond to expected future regulation. Misclassifying an anticipation period can contaminate baseline comparisons and requires a treatment-timing reconsideration.
hint: Consider when incentives changed, not only when enforcement began.

title: Cost-effectiveness with fixed health target
prompt: Two programs each avert exactly 10 comparable expected illness cases, with all other effects identical. A costs 40,000 and B costs 30,000. Which is more cost-effective?
correct: B, at 3,000 per case averted.
wrong: A, at 4,000 per case averted.
Both, because equal benefits imply equal costs.
Neither can be compared without monetizing a case.
explanation: With an identical specified outcome and no other differences, cost per case is sufficient: 4,000 for A and 3,000 for B. Monetization is needed for a net-benefit test, not this ranking.
hint: Divide each program’s cost by its common health outcome.

title: Break-even benefit estimate
prompt: A project costs 90 now and delivers one uncertain monetary benefit B in one year. Evaluation uses expected NPV, a 5% discount rate, and no other costs or benefits. What expected B makes NPV zero?
correct: 94.50 currency units.
wrong: 90.00 currency units.
85.71 currency units.
4.50 currency units.
explanation: Set −90 + E[B]/1.05 = 0, yielding E[B] = 94.50. This is a break-even expected-value calculation under the stipulated evaluation rule.
hint: Compound today’s cost for one year to find the required future benefit.
